title: fight over republican drawn congressional map missouri returns us supreme court 2026 09 09
text:
Sept 9 (Reuters) - Challengers to a redrawn congressional map in Missouri aimed at favoring Republicans ​asked the U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday to suspend a federal judge's order that allowed only ‌those reconfigured boundaries to be used in November's midterm elections.
The map's challengers, including a group opposed to the Republican-drawn map called People Not Politicians, made the request in an emergency filing, moving swiftly after St. Louis, Missouri-based Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued his decision ​on Tuesday.
The request brings the fight over Missouri's U.S. House of Representatives districts back to the Supreme ​Court just one day after it declined to intervene in a bid by Missouri officials to ⁠reinstate the redrawn map, which the state's top court had blocked until it is put to a referendum.
Clark's order ​appeared to conflict with the Missouri Supreme Court's unanimous September 3 ruling blocking the map, leaving the state's congressional districts in ​limbo and injecting further confusion into the high-stakes electoral fight.
Missouri Republicans adopted the new map, which dismantled the Kansas City-based seat of longtime Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver, in 2025 as part of a broader effort backed by President Donald Trump to redraw congressional districts in ways ​that could benefit Republican candidates.
Republicans hold a narrow 219-214 majority in the U.S. House, including one independent who caucuses ​with Republicans.
The dispute in Missouri arose when People Not Politicians, which calls itself a coalition of Republicans, Independents, and Democrats opposed to ‌gerrymandering the ⁠state's electoral map, collected enough signatures to file for a referendum under a provision in the state constitution that authorizes a ballot measure to approve any legislative act.
Hoskins rejected the petition, finding that state constitutional language does not apply to congressional redistricting.
The seven-member Missouri Supreme Court, which includes five Republican-appointed judges, disagreed, ruling that the referendum petition was "legal, ​sufficient, and timely," and that ​the redrawn map will ⁠not take effect until approved by voters.
Missouri Republican U.S. Representative Bob Onder and other plaintiffs then filed a lawsuit in federal court seeking to reinstate the Republican-drawn map.
In ​his order on Tuesday, Clark barred the use of any map for the November ​elections except for ⁠the redrawn 2025 map because those congressional district boundaries were already used for the August 4 primary elections.
The fight intensified after Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, the state's top election official, responded to Clark's order by telling local election officials ⁠to ​proceed with using the 2025 map.
The Missouri Supreme Court then said ​it would consider holding Hoskins in contempt if it determines he violated its September 3 ruling blocking that map. It ordered him to appear in ​person on September 10 for a hearing on the matter.
